title: Introduction to Internet
summary: ## What is the Internet?

The Internet (the Net) is a worldwide network of computer networks — an interconnection of large and small networks around the globe. With it you can exchange e-mail, transfer files and software, browse information on any topic, chat in real time, search databases, read news, send pictures and animation, and set up your own website.
## Getting connected
You need a PC with a browser, a telephone line or leased line, a modem and an account with an Internet Service Provider (ISP), who charges for installation and rent.
Dial-up — the most common basic connection: the computer dials a number given by the ISP and connects through the ISP's server; suited to a single PC or a small group.
ISDN (Integrated Services Digital Network) — like dial-up but over digital phone lines; two 64 Kbps channels give up to 128 Kbps, and you can make or receive calls on the same line while connected.

Leased line (direct Internet access) — a permanent, dedicated connection used by large institutions, companies and government agencies; the ISP places a router at your site to connect your local network to the Internet.

DSL (Digital Subscriber Line) broadband — an 'always-on' high-speed connection over the ordinary telephone wire; like ISDN you can use the phone while online. Wireless (Wi-Fi) connections need a Wi-Fi card.
## How does the Internet work?

Data (e.g. a web page) is broken into equal-sized packets. A header added to each packet says where it came from, where it is going and how it fits with the others. Packets travel from computer to computer; each decides the next hop, so packets may take different routes. At the destination they are checked and put back together in order. TCP/IP, the set of rules for this, is called the 'glue' of the Internet.
## Common terms

WWW (World Wide Web) — a collection of linked electronic documents (web pages) stored on servers around the world. Web server — a computer that stores web pages and serves them on request, connected 24×7; programs: IIS and Apache. Hyperlink — an element (usually underlined, coloured text or a button) that links to another place or document. HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) — the language of key words called tags used to write web pages. Web page — an electronic document written in HTML that can contain text, graphics, video, animation, sound and forms, with a unique URL. Website — one or more web pages of a company, institute or person; its first page is the home page (index.htm).

URL (Uniform Resource Locator) — the unique address of a page, e.g. http://www.learnthenet.com/english/glossary/url.htm: protocol (http), domain name (server), directory and file name. IP address — the unique number of each host, written xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx with each part from 0 to 255, e.g. 192.100.8.56. DNS (Domain Name System) — translates easy-to-remember domain names into IP addresses.
## Internet addresses

Read a domain name from the right: in www.nios.ac.in — www (World Wide Web), nios (host computer), ac (academic organisation), in (India). Organisational domains: ac (academic), com (commercial), edu (educational), gov (government), net (network resources), org (non-profit). Geographic domains: au (Australia), in (India), jp (Japan), uk (United Kingdom), us (United States).
## Browsers and downloading

A web browser (client software) requests pages from web servers and displays them, e.g. Internet Explorer, Netscape Navigator (today Chrome, Firefox, Edge). Steps: type the URL → the browser sends a request → the server processes it → the server responds with the page → the browser displays it.

Saving a web page: Text File (text only), Web Page HTML only (no images), Web Page Complete (HTML plus a folder of images), Web Archive single file (.mht). Downloading: click the download link → Save → choose a folder (e.g. Temporary Files) → after download double-click the file to install → delete the setup file to free space.
## Internet services
Search engine — a program that finds information meeting given criteria, e.g. Google, Yahoo, MSN Search, Ask Jeeves, AltaVista.

E-mail — a paperless, fast, cheap way of sending messages, letters, pictures and files, 24×7; free services: Gmail, Yahoo Mail, Hotmail, Rediffmail. Mail passes from mail server to mail server and waits in the recipient's mailbox. SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends mail and works with POP (Post Office Protocol) servers. An address such as sksharma@yahoo.com has a user ID, the @ sign and a domain (host) name ending in a top-level domain (TLD) such as .com. A message has a header (To, Cc, Bcc, Subject) and a body; Cc recipients are visible to all, Bcc recipients are hidden.

Telnet — a network protocol on the Internet or LAN that connects your PC to a server so that commands typed are executed on the server (remote access and control). FTP (File Transfer Protocol) — exchanges files over a TCP/IP network between an FTP server and a client: upload, download, rename, delete; it promotes sharing of files and transfers data reliably and efficiently.

vsa: What is the Internet? Write any two applications of it.
The Internet is a worldwide network of computer networks. Applications: exchanging e-mail, transferring files and software, browsing information, chatting, reading news, searching databases.
Differentiate between a website and a web page.

A web page is a single electronic document written in HTML with its own URL. A website is a collection of one or more related web pages belonging to an organisation or person; its first page is the home page.
What is a URL? Explain its parts with an example.

A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the unique address of a web page. In http://www.learnthenet.com/english/glossary/url.htm: http — protocol; www.learnthenet.com — domain name (server); /english/glossary/ — directory; url.htm — file name.
What are the two main parts of an e-mail address? Explain with an example.
In sksharma@yahoo.com, 'sksharma' is the user ID (mailbox) and 'yahoo.com' is the domain (host) name of the mail server, separated by @; '.com' is the top-level domain.

Explain the different types of Internet connections.

Dial-up — dial the ISP's number over a phone line; basic and common. ISDN — digital phone lines, up to 128 Kbps, phone usable while online. Leased line — permanent dedicated connection for large organisations, with a router at the site. DSL broadband — always-on, high speed over the phone wire. Wireless — Wi-Fi card, no cables.
What is a search engine? Name two search engines and give tips for searching.

A search engine is a program that finds information on the Web meeting given criteria and lists matching pages. Examples: Google, Yahoo. Tips: use specific key words, put exact phrases in quotes, add or remove words to narrow the results.
Write the steps to send an e-mail.

(1) Open the mail website and log in with user ID and password. (2) Click Compose. (3) Type the recipient's address in To (and Cc/Bcc if needed). (4) Type the subject. (5) Type the message in the body and attach files if needed. (6) Click Send.
Write the steps to download a file from the Internet.

(1) Create a folder such as Temporary Files. (2) Click the download link of the software. (3) Click Save and choose the folder. (4) Wait for the download to finish. (5) Double-click the file to install it, following the screens. (6) Delete the downloaded file to free space.
la: (a) Explain Telnet and FTP. (b) Explain organisational domains and geographical domains.

(a) Telnet is a network protocol used on the Internet or a LAN; the Telnet program connects your PC to a server so that commands you type run on the server, letting you control it remotely. FTP (File Transfer Protocol) is used to exchange files over a TCP/IP network: an FTP client connects to an FTP server to upload, download, rename or delete files.
(b) Organisational domains show the type of organisation: .ac, .com, .edu, .gov, .net, .org. Geographical domains are two-letter country codes: .in (India), .uk, .us, .au, .jp.

or: What happens to a piece of data when it is transferred over the Internet? Explain.

It is broken into equal-sized packets; a header saying where each packet came from, where it is going and how it fits with the others is added; each packet travels from computer to computer, each deciding the next hop, so packets may follow different routes; at the destination they are checked and reassembled in order.

la: (a) Define organisational domain. What are its types? (b) Explain the Domain Name System with an example.

(a) The organisational domain is the rightmost part of a domain name that shows the type of organisation: .ac (academic), .com (commercial), .edu (educational), .gov (government), .net (network resources), .org (non-profit). Geographic domains show the country: .in, .uk, .us, .au, .jp.
(b) Every computer on the Internet has a numeric IP address that is hard to remember. DNS (Domain Name System) gives each host a name and translates the name into its IP address. For example in www.nios.ac.in: www — World Wide Web, nios — host computer, ac — academic organisation, in — India.
(a) What is a web server? What is it responsible for? Name two web server programs. (b) Define a web page. What can a web page contain?

(a) A web server is a computer that stores web pages and is connected to the Internet round the clock. It accepts requests from users' browsers and serves them the web pages. Programs: IIS (Internet Information Server) and Apache.
(b) A web page is an electronic document written in HTML, with its own URL. It can contain text, graphics, video, animation and sound, and interactive features such as data entry forms, and hyperlinks to other pages.
(a) Differentiate between a web server and a web browser, with an example of each. (b) Explain the role of 'Cc' and 'Bcc' while composing an e-mail.

(a) A web server is a computer that stores web pages and serves them in response to users' requests, e.g. Apache, IIS. A web browser is the software on the user's computer that requests and displays web pages, e.g. Internet Explorer, Chrome.
(b) Cc (carbon copy) sends a copy to other people; all recipients can see who received it. Bcc (blind carbon copy) also sends a copy, but Bcc addresses are hidden from the To, Cc and other Bcc recipients.
(a) Define TCP/IP and HTML. (b) Explain how data is transferred over the Internet.

(a) TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol/Internet Protocol) is the set of rules by which computers on the Internet communicate; it is called the 'glue' of the Internet. HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) is the language of key words called tags used to write web pages.
(b) The data (e.g. a web page) is broken into many equal-sized pieces called packets. A header is added to each packet saying where it came from, where it is going and how it fits with the other packets. Each packet is sent from computer to computer (routers) until it reaches the destination; each computer on the way decides where to send it next, so packets may take different routes. At the destination the packets are checked and put back together in the right order.
Define WWW, hyperlink, web page, website and URL.

WWW — a collection of electronic documents (web pages) linked like a spider web and stored on servers worldwide. Hyperlink — an element that links to another place in the same or another document, shown as underlined coloured text or a button. Web page — an electronic document written in HTML that can contain text, graphics, video and sound, with a unique URL. Website — one or more web pages of an organisation or person; the first is the home page. URL — the unique address of a web page, e.g. http://www.nios.ac.in.
Explain how a browser connects to a website. Name two browsers.

(1) The user types a URL such as www.nios.ac.in in the browser. (2) The browser connects and sends a request to the web server. (3) The server receives and processes the request. (4) The server responds with the home page. (5) The browser displays the page and the connection is closed. Browsers: Internet Explorer, Netscape Navigator (today Chrome, Firefox).
